On the left wall, a broad cork board hung with papers and string. Most of the papers were gone or curled and yellow with age, but a few hung fresh. He took the paper off the board and carried it to the counter. The clerk set his ledger down, read it over, and gave Alaric a longer look than he had during registration. "Catacombs. First day." The warden's office keeps the upper stair clear down to the first level door, past that it's yours. First level's the shallow end, but it's still a dungeon. Things down there don't stay dead because you killed them once." He stamped the slip and held it out. "Seal turns READY when the level's cleared. Bring the slip back, we pay out a hundred and ten copper. No trophies wanted — the level being clear is the job." Alaric took the slip. The wax was still warm. "Old Crown runs deeper than one floor," the clerk added, reaching for the folder again. "Stairs go down. If you're on one and hear something from below, that's not your problem. Walk up." He was already turning to the dripping newcomer at the door. "Next." The slip was small enough to fold into a palm: the crossed sword-and-staff, the contract lines, the blank space where READY would go.

The road west out of Alderwatch was packed dirt, rutted by cartwheels, running between low stone walls with the morning mist still burning off the fields. A woodcutter's cart passed him going the other way, the driver giving the staff on Alaric's back a flat glance and nothing more. Crows worked a plowed field to the north. The ruined chapel showed itself long before the hour was out — a broken tower leaning over a gable roof gone moss-grey, sitting in a fold of land where the road bent toward a ford. He was still a good twenty minutes out when he saw the thing at the roadside. A dead dog, or what was left of one. Lay half in the ditch by the wall, and it had not died cleanly: the carcass was opened along the belly, but nothing had eaten it. No flies massed the way they should, no fox had dragged it off in the night, and the ground around it showed no tracks he could read — just a smear in the mud where something had been pulled, or had crawled, toward the wall and then stopped. The ditch grass nearby was flattened in a line, as if something heavy had gone along it westward, toward the chapel. Whatever had done this had left no print, no droppings, no hair snagged on the stones. The road itself stayed clear in both directions. The chapel smoke-hole, if it had ever had one, showed no smoke. From this distance the ruin sat quiet against the pale sky. The flattened grass led on toward the ford and the ruin. The dog lay where it was. The wall here was low enough to sit on, and the morning was warming.

extra.display_text:
The dog stayed where it was. Alaric walked on, and the flattened grass in the ditch ran beside the road a while before the wall ended and the land opened toward the ford. The chapel ruin sat above the water on a low rise, its yard ringed by a wall broken in two places. Inside the yard the grass was cut short, neater than anywhere else on the road — the warden's work, plainly kept. A few leaning marker stones stood among the grass, and the collapsed tower had spilled its rubble down the north gable like a rockslide frozen mid-fall. The doors of the chapel itself had rotted off their hinges; through the gap he could see a floor of bare flags and bird droppings. A man was kneeling by the yard wall when Alaric came up the path, trimming the grass along the stones with a short hook-blade. He rose slowly, one hand pressed to his lower back, and looked Alaric over — staff, robes, the red eyes. "Guild?" he said. "You'd be the first this month." He wiped the blade on his sleeve and sheathed it. "Name's Ossler, I keep the yard. Stair's through the chapel, down under the altar slab. Warden's men keep the top of it swept clear to the first level door — that far it's safe as a cellar. Past the door is yours, and I won't pretend I'd go past it for any coin the Guild prints." He tilted his head at the ruined tower. "It's been quiet up top a while. Quiet's not the same as empty, down there." He led the way through the rotted doors anyway, boots scraping on the flags. Beneath the fallen altar slab a stairwell opened into the dark, stone steps going down in a tight spiral, lantern hooks set into the wall every few turns, all of them empty. "There's oil in the crock by the door if you want light," Ossler said. "Door at the bottom's iron-banded. Warden's men shut it after themselves when they sweep. It opens outward." He lingered at the top of the steps, working his back with one knuckle, waiting to see whether the young mage meant to go down now or stand there thinking about it a while longer.

mes:
The dog stayed where it was. Alaric walked on, and the flattened grass in the ditch ran beside the road a while before the wall ended and the land opened toward the ford.

The chapel ruin sat above the water on a low rise, its yard ringed by a wall broken in two places. Inside the yard the grass was cut short, neater than anywhere else on the road — the warden's work, plainly kept. A few leaning marker stones stood among the grass, and the collapsed tower had spilled its rubble down the north gable like a rockslide frozen mid-fall. The doors of the chapel itself had rotted off their hinges; through the gap he could see a floor of bare flags and bird droppings.

A man was kneeling by the yard wall when Alaric came up the path, trimming the grass along the stones with a short hook-blade. He rose slowly, one hand pressed to his lower back, and looked Alaric over — staff, robes, the red eyes.

"Guild?" he said. "You'd be the first this month." He wiped the blade on his sleeve and sheathed it. "Name's Ossler, I keep the yard. Stair's through the chapel, down under the altar slab. Warden's men keep the top of it swept clear to the first level door — that far it's safe as a cellar. Past the door is yours, and I won't pretend I'd go past it for any coin the Guild prints." He tilted his head at the ruined tower. "It's been quiet up top a while. Quiet's not the same as empty, down there."

He led the way through the rotted doors anyway, boots scraping on the flags. Beneath the fallen altar slab a stairwell opened into the dark, stone steps going down in a tight spiral, lantern hooks set into the wall every few turns, all of them empty.

"There's oil in the crock by the door if you want light," Ossler said. "Door at the bottom's iron-banded. Warden's men shut it after themselves when they sweep. It opens outward." He lingered at the top of the steps, working his back with one knuckle, waiting to see whether the young mage meant to go down now or stand there thinking about it a while longer.

Alaric took the oil crock by the door, filled one of the empty lantern hooks' lamps from his fingers' fumbling, and got a stub of wick burning with a thought and a spark of his own making — easier than flint down here in the cold. Ossler watched the small blue flare of it without comment and went back to his grass. The stairs wound down in a tight spiral, each step worn shallow in the middle by feet long dead. The light swung shadows across the walls. Old mortar lines, a few scratched marks that might have been mason's tallies or something else, and every few turns a niche where a lamp had once sat, its bracket rusted to a stub. The air changed as he went — the damp grass-smell of the chapel giving way to something colder and stiller, stone that had not felt sun in centuries. His footsteps came back to him doubled off the curve of the stair. The sweep marks showed where the warden's men had kept their promise: the steps near the top were clean of dust, and the banister stone had been brushed. Deeper down, the dust thickened again, undisturbed, a grey felt over every surface. Nothing had come up this way in a while, and nothing had gone down either. The stair ended at a small square landing. Facing him was the door — iron-banded oak, older than anything above, its bands gone black with age but its hinges swept free of rust. It stood shut. A heavy iron ring hung in a cradle of brackets, and along the bottom edge of the door the dust lay in a smooth, unbroken seam. The air leaking around it was cold enough that his breath barely showed, and it carried a smell he could not put a name to — not rot exactly, more like a cellar where something had once been stored a very long time and then forgotten. The lamp guttered once in the draft under the door and steadied. The ring hung there, and the door waited.

Alaric took the oil crock by the door, filled one of the empty lantern hooks' lamps from his fingers' fumbling, and got a stub of wick burning with a thought and a spark of his own making — easier than flint down here in the cold. Ossler watched the small blue flare of it without comment and went back to his grass.

The stairs wound down in a tight spiral, each step worn shallow in the middle by feet long dead. The light swung shadows across the walls. Old mortar lines, a few scratched marks that might have been mason's tallies or something else, and every few turns a niche where a lamp had once sat, its bracket rusted to a stub. The air changed as he went — the damp grass-smell of the chapel giving way to something colder and stiller, stone that had not felt sun in centuries. His footsteps came back to him doubled off the curve of the stair.

The sweep marks showed where the warden's men had kept their promise: the steps near the top were clean of dust, and the banister stone had been brushed. Deeper down, the dust thickened again, undisturbed, a grey felt over every surface. Nothing had come up this way in a while, and nothing had gone down either.

The stair ended at a small square landing. Facing him was the door — iron-banded oak, older than anything above, its bands gone black with age but its hinges swept free of rust. It stood shut. A heavy iron ring hung in a cradle of brackets, and along the bottom edge of the door the dust lay in a smooth, unbroken seam.

The air leaking around it was cold enough that his breath barely showed, and it carried a smell he could not put a name to — not rot exactly, more like a cellar where something had once been stored a very long time and then forgotten.

The lamp guttered once in the draft under the door and steadied. The ring hung there, and the door waited.

It did not come nearer. It did not go away. Two ways led on. A broad arch at the back of the hall opened onto a corridor running straight into the dark, the warden's chalk arrow pointing down it. To the left, between two pillars, a narrower passage sloped down by shallow steps toward the sound of the dragging, its mouth hung with a curtain of rotted chain links that stirred faintly in the air the dragging made. He was not alone in the quiet. From somewhere off to the left, past the far pillars, came a sound like a slow dry dragging — a scrape, a pause, a scrape — rhythmic as a man pacing, though slower than any pacing he had heard. It did not come nearer. It did not go away.

Two ways led on. A broad arch at the back of the hall opened onto a corridor running straight into the dark, the warden's chalk arrow pointing down it. To the left, between two pillars, a narrower passage sloped down by shallow steps toward the sound of the dragging, its mouth hung with a curtain of rotted chain links that stirred faintly in the air the dragging made.

The lamp burned steady. The dead in their niches kept still.
